set.st: On the night of Friday 20 September 1889 nearly $40,000 of express-company money was taken from the vault of the Iron Exchange Bank at Hurley, opened with the combination. It was an inside job: in November 1889 the bank's bookkeeper and an Ironwood saloonkeeper were arrested; the saloonkeeper was convicted at Ashland in June 1890 and served five years at Waupun. The amount was put at $39,000 and only about $1,100 was ever recovered. An 1898 retrospective put the total at $41,000 and recalled that in 1890 the bookkeeper's stepfather, a New London banker, had been convicted of passing $300 of the stolen bills, which were musty and stained as if they had lain buried, so at least part of the cache had been dug up within a year. When he was released in April 1895 the Marinette Eagle reported the detectives' belief that the money had been carried to some point north of Hurley and buried, or sunk in a watertight box in the Montreal River; a Duluth paper the same week said buried in Ashland or Iron County or sunk in the river. No find was ever reported.
set.tovw: Lead grade D: period papers confirm the 1889 theft and that most of the $39,000-41,000 was never recovered, and stained bills passed in 1890 suggest the money was indeed buried; the river-or-north-of-Hurley location rests on one 1895 detectives' theory, so no place closer than the town
